content: Atopic eczema, also referred to as atopic dermatitis, is a chronic inflammatory skin condition that significantly impacts patients' quality of life. Phototherapy is sometimes employed as a treatment option when topical therapies, such as corticosteroids, are either ineffective or poorly tolerated. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of phototherapy in managing atopic eczema. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Skin Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and ClinicalTrials.gov, up to January 2021. The analysis included randomized controlled trials involving both adults and children with clinically diagnosed atopic eczema, regardless of subtype or severity. Comparisons were made between various types of phototherapy and other treatments, including placebo, no treatment, or alternative therapies. The review included 32 trials with a total of 1,219 participants, aged between 5 and 83 years (mean age: 28 years), with an equal distribution of males and females. Most participants were recruited from secondary care dermatology clinics, and the average study duration was 13 weeks, ranging from 10 days to one year. The interventions assessed included narrowband ultraviolet B (NB-UVB), ultraviolet A1 (UVA1), broadband ultraviolet B (BB-UVB), ultraviolet AB (UVAB), psoralen plus ultraviolet A (PUVA), ultraviolet A (UVA), unspecified ultraviolet B (UVB), full-spectrum light, Saalmann selective ultraviolet phototherapy (SUP) cabin, saltwater bath plus UVB (balneophototherapy), and excimer laser. Comparators included placebo, no treatment, other phototherapy modalities, topical treatments, or varying doses of the same phototherapy. Key Findings: NB-UVB versus Placebo/No Treatment: Physician-Assessed Signs: NB-UVB may lead to a greater reduction in physician-assessed signs of atopic eczema compared to placebo after 12 weeks of treatment (mean difference [MD] -9.4, 95% confidence interval [CI] -3.62 to -15.18; 1 trial, 41 participants). However, two trials reported minimal differences between NB-UVB and no treatment over 4-6 weeks, while another trial showed improved signs with NB-UVB after 9 weeks. Patient-Reported Itch: NB-UVB may increase the number of participants reporting reduced itch after 12 weeks compared to placebo (risk ratio [RR] 1.72, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.69; 1 trial, 40 participants). However, another trial found little difference in itch severity after 4 weeks. Global Improvement: The proportion of participants experiencing moderate or greater global improvement may be higher with NB-UVB than placebo after 12 weeks (RR 2.81, 95% CI 1.10 to 7.17; 1 trial, 41 participants). Adverse Events: NB-UVB may not significantly affect withdrawal rates due to adverse events. No withdrawals were reported in one trial (18 participants, 9 weeks), while two trials comparing NB-UVB to no treatment each reported one withdrawal per group (71 participants, 8-12 weeks). Certainty of Evidence: All reported outcomes were supported by low-certainty evidence due to concerns about bias and imprecision. No trials reported health-related quality of life (HRQoL). NB-UVB versus UVA1: Physician-Assessed Signs: There was no evidence of a difference in physician-assessed signs after 6 weeks (MD -2.00, 95% CI -8.41 to 4.41; 1 trial, 46 participants). Two split-body trials (20 participants, 40 sides) reported lower scores with NB-UVB at 7-8 weeks. Patient-Reported Itch: No significant difference in itch severity was observed after 6 weeks (MD 0.3, 95% CI -1.07 to 1.67; 1 trial, 46 participants). HRQoL: One trial reported HRQoL at 6 weeks (MD 2.9, 95% CI -9.57 to 15.37; 1 trial, 46 participants). Adverse Events: One split-body trial reported no withdrawals due to adverse events over 12 weeks (13 participants). Certainty of Evidence: The evidence for all outcomes was judged to be of very low certainty due to bias and imprecision. NB-UVB versus PUVA: Physician-Assessed Signs: No significant difference was observed in physician-assessed signs after 6 weeks (64.1% reduction with NB-UVB versus 65.7% reduction with PUVA; 1 trial, 10 participants, 20 sides). Global Improvement: No evidence of a difference in marked improvement or complete remission after 6 weeks (odds ratio [OR] 1.00, 95% CI 0.13 to 7.89; 1 trial, 9/10 participants with both treatments). Adverse Events: One split-body trial reported no withdrawals due to adverse events in 10 participants over 6 weeks. Certainty of Evidence: The evidence for all outcomes was of very low certainty due to bias and imprecision. Patient-reported symptoms and HRQoL were not reported. UVA1 versus PUVA: Physician-Assessed Signs: PUVA (oral 5-methoxypsoralen plus UVA) may reduce physician-assessed signs more than UVA1 after 3 weeks (MD 11.3, 95% CI -0.21 to 22.81; 1 trial, 40 participants). However, the evidence was of very low certainty due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. Other Outcomes: Patient-reported symptoms, global improvement, HRQoL, and adverse events were not reported. Adverse Events: Reported adverse events across trials included low rates of phototoxic reactions, severe irritation, UV burns, bacterial superinfection, disease exacerbation, and eczema herpeticum. Authors' Conclusions: NB-UVB may improve physician-assessed signs, patient-reported symptoms, and global improvement compared to placebo or no treatment after 12 weeks, without a significant difference in withdrawal rates due to adverse events. However, the certainty of evidence for these findings is low. Evidence comparing NB-UVB to UVA1 or PUVA, and UVA1 to PUVA, is of very low certainty. Further research is needed to better understand the safety and efficacy of phototherapy for atopic eczema.
